To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) compared to younger adults, older adults performed more poorly on a description-based decision-making task but performed similarly on an experience-based decision-making task; (2) age differences in performance on the description-based decision-making were explained by deliberative abilities; and (3) on the experience-based decision-making, older adults reported greater use of affect-based decision strategies compared to younger adults.
older adults performed more poorly on a description-based decision-making task, but performed similarly on an experience-based decision-making task.
older adults experience declines in their deliberative decision-making abilities, but their experiential decision-making abilities remain intact.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how older adults make decisions in situations where they are provided with explicit information versus situations where they must rely on past experiences.
understanding how age differences in decision-making abilities may be explained by age-related declines in deliberative versus experiential processing.
how age differences in decision-making processes affect the way that older and younger adults make decisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this study support the idea that older adults are more likely to rely on experiential processes in decision making, but they are less able to rely on deliberative processes.
older adults perform worse than younger adults on description-based tasks that emphasize deliberative processes, but perform comparably to younger adults on experience-based tasks.
older adults are more likely to use experiential strategies than younger adults, and that age-related differences are likely to emerge on tasks that require deliberate processing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
age-related declines in deliberative processes can be observed in description-based decision tasks but not in experience-based tasks.

age-related differences are most pronounced when decision-making tasks are highly reliant on deliberative processing and that older adults are more likely to rely on experiential processing when making decisions.

the age differences in decision making are not uniform across different types of tasks, and that age differences in decision-making performance are more likely to occur in tasks that rely on deliberative processes than in those that rely on experiential processes. The main takeaway from our work is that
older adults are able to make decisions based on experience, but are less able to do so based on description.
the experiential-deliberative framework provides a useful way of thinking about age differences in decision making.
age effects in decision-making tasks are not universal.
